title: Tides run on the Moon's clock
slideTitles: Tides run on the Moon's clock
Boston gets two high tides a day.
The Moon stretches the ocean into two bulges.
The Sun makes the tide grow and shrink.
Coastline shape decides how high the tide climbs.

states.lead: Water level, hour by hour, for two days.
states.body: NOAA prediction for Boston Harbor, June 11 and 12, 2025, in meters above mean lower low water.

states.lead: High tides arrive 12 h 25 min apart.
states.body: That is the average gap between every Boston high tide from January 10 to 31, 2025.
Two tides take 24 hours 50 minutes, the time Earth needs to turn back under the Moon.

states.lead: The Moon pulls the near ocean hardest.
states.body: Gravity weakens with distance, so water facing the Moon is pulled more than Earth's center.

states.lead: The far ocean is pulled least.
states.body: Earth is pulled away from that water, which leaves a second bulge on the opposite side.
One turn back under the Moon takes 24 hours 50 minutes, so both bulges pass each coast.

states.lead: Every Boston high and low for three weeks.
states.body: NOAA predictions, January 10 to 31, 2025. The zigzag widens and narrows on a two week rhythm.

states.lead: Sun and Moon in line: spring tides.
states.body: At full and new moon their pulls add, and a single swing reaches 3.6 m.

states.lead: Sun and Moon at right angles: neap tides.
states.body: The Sun's tidal pull is 46% of the Moon's and now works against it. Swings shrink to 1.8 m.
Average gap between high and low water at five NOAA stations, 1983 to 2001.

states.lead: Funnel-shaped bays get the biggest tides.
states.body: Anchorage, at the head of Cook Inlet, averages 8.0 m. Eastport sits at the Bay of Fundy's mouth.
It averages 0.37 m. Anchorage's range is 22 times larger.
